DC Judge Permanently Closes Reflecting Pool Case Against MD Olympian
Maryland Olympian David Hearn had been accused of vandalizing the Reflecting Pool in June while he was inspecting its peeling sealant.
BETHESDA, MD — A judge permanently dismissed a criminal case on Thursday that was tied to Maryland Olympian David Hearn, who was accused of vandalizing the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool over the summer.
Although the Justice Department dismissed the vandalism case in July, a D.C. Superior Court order by Judge Todd Edelman bars prosecutors from refiling the same charges against Hearn.
In his decision, Edelman cited potential pressure from the Trump administration.

"While the government wishes to hold open the possibility of the development of evidence that would support a future prosecution, its own representations make plain that such a possibility is theoretical at best, and more likely, is simply fanciful," the order reads.
"... this case must be dismissed with prejudice, and the government must thus be barred from reinstituting this charge against Mr. Hearn."
Find out what's happening in Bethesda-Chevy Chasefor free with the latest updates from Patch.
The 67-year-old Bethesda resident had been indicted on a felony charge of destruction of property after prosecutors argued Hearn caused more than $1,000 in damage when he reached into the Reflecting Pool to examine a piece of sealant that had peeled off.
Hearn said he was on a bike ride on June 19 when he examined the sealant, adding that he obeyed a park worker’s command to let go.
The Justice Department ultimately dropped the case after the Interior Department found the Reflecting Pool damage was caused by rushed contractor work.

The sealant is tied to the $14 million rehabilitation project the Trump administration undertook ahead of the nation's 250th anniversary. President Donald Trump previously said multiple individuals were arrested for "vandalizing" the Reflecting Pool.
Hearn’s attorneys said the ruling is "a victory for the rule of law and for an innocent American seeking justice" and allows Hearn to "move forward with his life as he deserves."
"This administration chose to pursue an unjust prosecution against Mr. Hearn. It should not get repeated chances to wield the power of criminal prosecution against someone who should never have been prosecuted," the lawyers said in a statement.
Hearn had competed in three Summer Olympics, earning his best finish, ninth, at the 1996 Atlanta Olympic Games, the U.S. Olympic and Paralympic Committee says on its website.
The Associated Press contributed to this report.

A judge on Thursday permanently dismissed the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool vandalism case against former Olympian David Hearn, who was accused of damaging the costly $14 million renovation project in June.
D.C. Superior Court Judge Todd Edelman’s ruling marks the end of a monthslong legal battle that included President Donald Trump criticizing U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro after she moved to voluntarily dismiss the federal charges in late July.
Unlike Pirro’s decision, Thursday’s ruling was made with prejudice, meaning the Department of Justice (DOJ) cannot refile the same charges against Hearn.

Hearn’s counsel described the decision as a victory for “an innocent American seeking justice.”

Hearn was arrested on June 19 and later indicted on one felony count of destruction of property for allegedly damaging the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool’s lining.
Prosecutors alleged that Hearn was seen grabbing and tugging on a loose section of the pool’s coating, reportedly causing about $1,000 in damage. Officials added that he continued to do so even after National Park Service employees urged him to stop.

“Anybody who thinks the Reflecting Pool wasn’t vandalized should go back to Law School!” Trump previously said in a post on Truth Social.
“People were on their knees with their hands in the water at the exact location of the ‘slashes.’ Additionally, there were witnesses to the VANDALISM, and the flexible areas of the material were cut with a knife,” he added.
The DOJ moved to dismiss the indictment after evidence from the Department of the Interior revealed that the damage was caused by a “rushed and botched” installation by contractor Atlantic Industrial Coatings ahead of the America 250 celebrations, court filings said.

D.C. Judge Dismisses Reflecting Pool Charges — with Prejudice
Judge Throws Out Reflecting Pool Damage Case Against Ex-Olympian
sources.text:
A judge in Washington on Oct. 1 dismissed a criminal case against David Hearn, a former U.S. Olympian, with prejudice.
That means that federal prosecutors, who requested that the case be thrown out without prejudice, cannot refile charges in the future.
“A dismissal without prejudice would not account for the exceptional circumstances presented by this case,” Judge Todd Edelman of the Superior Court of the District of Columbia wrote in a 26-page order.
Lawyers representing Hearn, 67, celebrated the move.
“This decision is a victory for the rule of law and for an innocent American seeking justice,” they said in a statement.
“This administration chose to pursue an unjust prosecution against Mr. Hearn. It should not get repeated chances to wield the power of criminal prosecution against someone who should never have been prosecuted. Today’s decision protects Mr. Hearn from that threat, allowing him to move forward with his life as he deserves.”
Hearn was charged for allegedly vandalizing the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool.
Lawyers for Hearn then told the judge that the dismissal should be without prejudice, arguing that the move would prevent Hearn from “continued harassment based on the same discredited allegations” against him, and referenced reports suggesting that prosecutors were planning to bring new charges against the former Olympian canoe slalomist.
The U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Columbia said that the dismissal should be without prejudice, in part because Hearn was observed placing his hands in the pool and pulling on its liner.
“The caselaw makes clear that dismissal without prejudice is the default precisely because additional evidence of guilt could come to light before the statute of limitations expires,” prosecutors said. “The mere potential that charges may be re-brought does not constitute the type of harassment for which a dismissal with prejudice is appropriate.”
Edelman said that the prospect of future charges against Hearn was unlikely. He also referenced how President Donald Trump criticized the decision to move for dismissal and called for reinstating the prosecution.
“While all defendants deal with some degree of uncertainty regarding the odds of re-prosecution after a case has been dismissed, Mr. Hearn faces the unique possibility that the government will revive this case—one that it has already announced to be meritless—based on political pressure brought by the President of the United States upon his subordinate officers,” the judge wrote.
“The Court respects the authority of the Office of the United States Attorney to decide which cases to prosecute and which to dismiss. However, in the exceptional circumstances posed by this case, the government has no right to retain the ability to compound the errors it has already made, or even to threaten to do so, at Mr. Hearn’s expense.”

Judge blocks federal prosecutors from refiling charges in Reflecting Pool case
A worker cleans the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool on June 25, 2026. (Photo by Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)
WASHINGTON — A D.C. Superior Court judge ruled Thursday that prosecutors cannot, for a second time, charge former Olympic canoeist David Hearn with damaging the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool.
Judge Todd E. Edelman wrote in his ruling that “the observed damage to the Reflecting Pool was due to a contractor’s ‘rushed and botched’ installation of the lining while conducting renovations, and Mr. Hearn’s actions had no effect on the value of the Pool.”
U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia Jeanine Pirro sought to drop the charges against Hearn, of Maryland, in August, writing in a brief to the court that she wouldn’t have filed a case against him had she had more information from the Interior Department, which manages the Reflecting Pool.
“Specifically, the newly released documents reveal that work on installing the lining almost immediately fell behind, due to a combination of very rainy and windy weather, repeated failures of testing on the sealing of the expansion joints, and delays in obtaining sealing product at the worksite,” Pirro wrote. “The rush to complete the project led to hasty and botched work that was not remediated before the project was finished and the fencing removed.”
But Edelman had to hold a hearing on the future of the case in early September after federal prosecutors signaled they may try to refile the charges.
The judge’s 26-page ruling blocks that from happening.
“The Court respects the authority of the Office of the United States Attorney to decide which cases to prosecute and which to dismiss,” Edelman wrote. “However, in the exceptional circumstances posed by this case, the government has no right to retain the ability to compound the errors it has already made, or even to threaten to do so, at Mr. Hearn’s expense.”

Olympic canoeist David Hearn has Reflecting Pool vandalism case tossed by judge with prejudice
See more of our coverage in your search results.
WASHINGTON — A DC judge on Thursday tossed the Trump administration’s case against former Olympic canoeist David Hearn for allegedly vandalizing the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool in June.
DC Superior Court Judge Todd Edelman dismissed with prejudice the felony count of destruction of property against the 67-year-old Olympian, meaning US Attorney Jeanine Pirro’s Office won’t be able to refile it.
“While the government wishes to hold open the possibility of the development of evidence that would support a future prosecution, its own representations make plain that such a possibility is theoretical at best, and more likely, is simply fanciful,” wrote Edelman.
The judge also claimed that Pirro’s office had “shot first and asked questions later” by charging Hearn in a “a lightning-fast indictment process.”
“Although the prosecutors assigned to this case have deemed it meritless, the President of the United States has repeatedly disparaged them and pressured them to change course,” Edelman added.
Hearn’s defense attorney Steve Levin praised the decision.
“We are gratified by the Court’s decision dismissing this case with prejudice,” Levin said in a statement. “Our justice system depends on prosecutors exercising independent judgment, free from political pressure, and on courts willing to safeguard that principle.”
“Today’s decision reaffirms the importance of those protections. We are proud to have stood beside Mr. Hearn in defending his rights and are pleased that he can finally put this matter behind him,” added Levin.
Prosecutors dropped their case in July, writing in court papers that the Interior Department failed to share information about its “flawed installation by the contractor” beforehand.
The decision enraged President Trump, who shot back in a post on Truth Social: “There may have been some contractor difficulty, but the major damage was caused by VANDALS!”
“I was disappointed in Jeanine Pirro. Really disappointed in Jeanine Pirro,” he also told reporters in August. “She folded like an umbrella.”
For a time, Pirro’s job appeared to be on the line as she was summoned to a tense Oval Office meeting with the president and Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, who denied that his team failed to provide evidence of the alleged vandalism in a timely fashion to DC prosecutors.
Hearn, who faced up to 10 years in prison upon conviction, had yanked at a flapping piece of lining at the bottom of the Reflecting Pool on June 19, before being told to stop by authorities.
But the sealant put down began peeling “[a]lmost immediately” after the contractor, Atlantic Industrial Coatings, had completed its work in anticipation of America 250 Independence Day festivities.
DOI assessed that Hearn’s tugging at the pool’s lining caused $1,000 worth of damage in statements made to Pirro’s office — despite a National Park Service engineer being “alerted to the peeling of the Reflecting Pool lining” by itself at least 10 days before the incident on June 9.
Hearn competed in three Summer Olympics as a US canoeist, earning ninth place at the 1996 games in Atlanta.
With Post wires

David Hearn case: Why did judge permanently dismiss ex-Olympian's reflecting pool case?
A Washington judge has permanently dismissed the criminal case against former Olympian David Hearn over damage to the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool.
WASHINGTON (AP) — A judge in the nation’s capital agreed on Thursday to permanently dismiss a criminal case charging a former Olympian with vandalizing the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, a move that could prevent federal prosecutors from reviving the case under political pressure from President Donald Trump.
D.C. Superior Court Judge Todd Edelman ordered the dismissal of David Hearn’s case with “prejudice,” which would block U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro’s office from refiling the felony charge against him. The judge ruled nearly a month after hearing attorneys’ arguments.
Hearn’s lawyers say Trump administration officials have continued to falsely accuse the Maryland resident of vandalizing the reflecting pool despite Pirro’s decision to drop the case on July 31. Trump responded by saying Pirro “choked” and “folded like an umbrella.”
Edelman said the case presents “exceptional circumstances” that warrant dismissing the case permanently. He agreed with defense attorneys that the government “shot first and asked questions later” by charging Hearn in a “a lightning-fast indictment process.”
“While the government wishes to hold open the possibility of the development of evidence that would support a future prosecution, its own representations make plain that such a possibility is theoretical at best, and more likely, is simply fanciful,” the judge wrote.
Permanently dismissing the case protects Hearn from prosecutors electing to revive the case under political pressure from Trump, the judge said.
“Although the prosecutors assigned to this case have deemed it meritless, the President of the United States has repeatedly disparaged them and pressured them to change course,” Edelman wrote.
In a court filing in July, Pirro said new evidence produced by the Interior Department showed Hearn wasn’t responsible for damage to the pool’s lining. Pirro’s office attributed the damage instead to a botched installation by a contractor as well as a rush to complete the project in time for this summer’s America 250 celebration in Washington.
Pirro’s admission was an embarrassing setback for the White House. Interior Secretary Doug Burgum has backed Trump’s claims that vandals damaged the pool.
Hearn has said he was on a bike ride on June 19 when he reached in to examine the pool’s newly peeled coating and briefly touched a chunk attached to the side of the pool. But he said he obeyed a park worker’s command to let go of it.
Hearn was charged with one count of property destruction, which carries a maximum prison sentence of 10 years. His lawyers questioned whether prosecutors properly presented the grand jury with adequate evidence to support the charge and the amount of damage alleged by the government.
Hearn, 67, of Bethesda, Maryland, competed in three Summer Olympics, earning his best finish, ninth, at the 1996 Atlanta Olympic Games, the U.S. Olympic and Paralympic Committee says on its website.
Trump, a Republican, appointed Pirro, a former Fox News host, to serve as the top federal prosecutor for the District of Columbia. Edelman was nominated to the bench by Democratic President Barack Obama.
Hearn’s attorneys said the ruling is “a victory for the rule of law and for an innocent American seeking justice” and allows Hearn to “move forward with his life as he deserves.”
“This administration chose to pursue an unjust prosecution against Mr. Hearn. It should not get repeated chances to wield the power of criminal prosecution against someone who should never have been prosecuted,” the lawyers said in a statement.

U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia Jeanine Pirro's office later moved to drop the charges after the Department of the Interior shared evidence showing the pool's damage resulted from "flawed installation," not vandalism. A court filing from Pirro's office stated that the indictment would never have been pursued if the Interior Department had disclosed the evidence it already held.
Trump, who ordered renovations to the pool, rejected that conclusion and publicly criticized Pirro for abandoning the case, saying she "folded like an umbrella" and "choked," according to Axios. Pirro's office sought a without-prejudice dismissal, a posture that would have kept the door open for prosecutors to bring fresh charges at a later date. At a September hearing, Assistant U.S. Attorney Michael Spence argued that the public had an interest in preserving the grand jury's ability to act on any future evidence, yet when pressed by the judge he could not offer even a theoretical scenario that might rescue the case.
Edelman rejected that position. "The government has no right to retain the ability to compound the errors it has already made, or even to threaten to do so, at Mr. Hearn's expense," he wrote.
In a joint statement, Hearn's legal team — Norm Eisen, Mary Dohrmann, Steve Levin, and Michael Bromwich — celebrated the outcome as "a victory for the rule of law and for an innocent American seeking justice" and said the prosecution should never have been initiated. I confess I always expected that Judge Todd Edelman would dismiss, with prejudice, the case charging Davey Hearn with damaging the reflecting pool. It was simply a too volatile case to leave Hearn hanging. I just didn’t know how he’d do it: Whether he’d comment on the seeming false claims from a National Park witness or misconduct from Jeanine Pirro’s people, or simply write a cautious opinion.
His opinion dismissing the case with prejudice is fairly modest — and as such will be virtually unassailable if Jeanine Pirro or some replacement flunky decides to do Trump’s bidding again. It endorses no claims of misconduct from Hearn’s team, however well substantiated (though it does gently question Pirro’s claim they rushed to indict this to deter others, noting that most Superior Court cases take most of the nine months they have to indict). With one exception (his citation of a NYT story describing the contractor taking blame, which came out on September 11), he relies exclusively on the evidence the government and Hearn (in a still-sealed exhibit) submitted about the renovation. Even where it cites Donald Trump’s interference in the case — and that’s almost the entirety of where Edelman places the responsibility for his decision — Edelman explicitly “has set aside descriptions of the President’s non-public statements and thought processes that appear in various news articles cited by the defense.”
But after listing 6 of Donald Trump’s rants in the wake of the dismissal of this case, Edelman then points to Trump’s lingering threat as the ongoing harm, including a harm that might chill political activism, that necessitates dismissing with prejudice.
But in this case, Mr. Hearn faces an additional—and practically unprecedented— type and degree of risk should the Court dismiss this case without prejudice. As elucidated supra, the government has conceded that its prosecution of Mr. Hearn was meritless and cannot identify any potential evidence or avenue of investigation that would allow it to reinstitute the case in good faith. Additionally, Mr. Hearn would have to await the decision as to whether the government revives a criminal case against him knowing that should he engage in political activity, his conduct could be viewed by the President as a reason to reinstate the prosecution. Edelman says Hearn’s case is “practically unprecedented.” But then he limits his comparators to what he knows, the DC Superior Court.
Because, of course, Hearn is not unique. Judges all over the country are struggling with how to achieve justice in these wildly politicized cases.
And to that end, Edelman repeats one thing over and over: No crime was committed.
Because that’s the kind of judgment that Hearn can use to pursue further justice.

“The Court agrees with the defense that in securing the Indictment against Mr. Hearn, the government shot first and asked questions later.”

The judge repeats more than just “no crime was committed.” He also describes the repeated threats of the president against Hearn, specific DOJ prosecutors, and those with whom he disagrees politically.

Pirro's admission was an embarrassing setback for the White House. Interior Secretary Doug Burgum has backed Trump's claims that vandals damaged the pool.

Judge blocks federal prosecutors from refiling charges in Reflecting Pool case
A worker cleans the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool on June 25, 2026. (Photo by Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)
WASHINGTON — A D.C. Superior Court judge ruled Thursday that prosecutors cannot, for a second time, charge former Olympic canoeist David Hearn with damaging the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool.
Judge Todd E. Edelman wrote in his ruling that “the observed damage to the Reflecting Pool was due to a contractor’s ‘rushed and botched’ installation of the lining while conducting renovations, and Mr. Hearn’s actions had no effect on the value of the Pool.”
U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia Jeanine Pirro sought to drop the charges against Hearn, of Maryland, in August, writing in a brief to the court that she wouldn’t have filed a case against him had she had more information from the Interior Department, which manages the Reflecting Pool.
“Specifically, the newly released documents reveal that work on installing the lining almost immediately fell behind, due to a combination of very rainy and windy weather, repeated failures of testing on the sealing of the expansion joints, and delays in obtaining sealing product at the worksite,” Pirro wrote. “The rush to complete the project led to hasty and botched work that was not remediated before the project was finished and the fencing removed.”
But Edelman had to hold a hearing on the future of the case in early September after federal prosecutors signaled they may try to refile the charges.
The judge’s 26-page ruling blocks that from happening.
“The Court respects the authority of the Office of the United States Attorney to decide which cases to prosecute and which to dismiss,” Edelman wrote. “However, in the exceptional circumstances posed by this case, the government has no right to retain the ability to compound the errors it has already made, or even to threaten to do so, at Mr. Hearn’s expense.”

Reflecting Pool vandalism charges against Olympic canoeist David Hearn permanently dismissed
A Washington, D.C., judge permanently dismissed the criminal indictment against U.S. Olympic canoeist David Hearn Thursday, ending a months-long saga around allegations of vandalism to the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool after the government admitted to a "botched" construction job in recent renovations.
In August, federal prosecutors asked Superior Court Judge Todd Edelman to dismiss the criminal indictment against Hearn, who had been charged with felony destruction of government property. He was accused of causing more than $1,000 in damage to the sealant that was installed last summer at the bottom of the Reflecting Pool.
Hearn pleaded not guilty to the charges, saying he had stopped by the pool in July while on a 64-mile bike ride through the nation's capital. He said he was arrested after he reached down into the pool and was detained for five hours.
The project to renovate the pool has been championed by President Trump, who in April launched an effort to address the pool's "terrible" condition, part of a slate of spring cleaning projects in Washington, D.C., ahead of the nation's 250th birthday. He had the pool's stone flooring coated with a sealant he called the "latest and greatest filament" and an "industrial-grade" variation of swimming pool liner. He told reporters he personally chose the sealant's color: "American Flag Blue."
The U.S. Attorney's Office in D.C. admitted in court filings that Hearn had not, in fact, damaged the pool, although U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro alleged in a July press conference that he had. Prosecutors said new information had come to light revealing the rips and tears in the pool lining were caused by a contractor's "botched installation."
Edelman dismissed the case shortly after the government's motion, but had not ruled on whether the case would be dismissed with prejudice, meaning the case could not be brought again, or without prejudice, meaning the charges could be revived. Hearn's lawyers said the charges should be dismissed with prejudice, while Pirro's office argued for a dismissal without prejudice.
Hearn's case, Edelman wrote, "presents a markedly different scenario" than the typical dismissal of criminal cases in federal court, because "within a month, the government recognized that its prosecution lacked merit."
"It reached this conclusion not because it has misidentified Mr. Hearn as the perpetrator of the alleged act, but because no crime had occurred," Edelman wrote, adding that the government's interest in keeping the possibility of charging Hearn again would result in a "meritless, politically motivated prosecution."
After Pirro's office moved to drop the case, Mr. Trump publicly rebuked his hand-picked D.C. prosecutor, saying that she had "choked" and "made a mistake" with the decision.
"I was disappointed with Jeanine Pirro," Mr. Trump told reporters in August. The president has frequently insisted the peeling was caused by vandals, not by problems with the more than $10 million project. "Who would do such a thing?" the president wrote in a Truth Social post on June 20 that also mentioned several arrests. Many of the other defendants accused of vandalizing the Reflecting Pool also had the charges against them dropped.
Pirro later made a bid to prove to Mr. Trump that the damage to the Reflecting Pool was caused by the shoddy construction job, bringing a box full of evidence to the White House that sources said contained all of the evidence collected from the Interior Department exculpating Hearn and several others from criminal vandalism.
The New York Times in September reported that the contractor, Atlantic Industrial Coatings, admitted in government documents that the workers had not used enough primer and that the pool liner that was applied contained two chemicals that were incompatible.
Days after Pirro's office moved to dismiss the case, CBS News reported that White House officials asked the Justice Department to weigh whether it would be possible to bring a new criminal case against Hearn.
In a statement, Norm Eisen, an attorney for Hearn, said that Edelman's ruling is "a victory for the rule of law and for an innocent American seeking justice."
"This case never should have been brought in the first place," Eisen said, adding that the prosecution was a "miscarriage of justice" and an "outrage that should shock every American."
A spokesperson for Pirro's office did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Edelman's decision.

sources.text:
A Washington judge permanently dismissed the criminal case against former U.S. Olympian David Hearn on Thursday, preventing federal prosecutors from reviving a felony vandalism charge that collapsed after the Justice Department acknowledged that faulty construction—not vandalism—caused damage to the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool.
D.C. Superior Court Judge Todd Edelman dismissed Hearn’s case “with prejudice,” meaning prosecutors cannot refile the same charge against the 67-year-old former Olympic canoeist. The ruling came after the government previously moved to abandon the prosecution but sought to preserve its ability to bring the case again.
Hearn’s prosecution had drawn national attention after U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro’s office accused him of “forcefully and violently” tearing material from the newly resurfaced Reflecting Pool.
President Donald Trump also repeatedly blamed vandals for the damage and publicly criticized Pirro after her office reversed course and moved to dismiss Hearn’s case.
The Justice Department ultimately acknowledged that evidence supplied after Hearn’s indictment showed that widespread peeling in the Reflecting Pool resulted from a rushed and flawed installation by a contractor.
In Thursday’s ruling, Edelman noted that the government had effectively acknowledged that “no crime had occurred.”
Judge closes the door on another prosecution
Hearn’s case had technically been dismissed since August.
What remained unresolved was whether prosecutors would be allowed to charge him again.
Pirro’s office asked for the original felony case to be dismissed without prejudice, which would have preserved that option. Hearn’s attorneys argued that leaving the possibility of another prosecution hanging over their client was unjustified after the government conceded that the evidence underlying the case had fallen apart.
At a September hearing, Edelman pressed Assistant U.S. Attorney Michael Spence to identify evidence that could conceivably revive the prosecution.
“Give me an example of one possible thing that could happen that would make this a viable prosecution or would allow you to explore going forward in the case,” Edelman said.
Spence acknowledged that he did not have a “very satisfying answer,” although he suggested repairs to the Reflecting Pool could theoretically uncover new evidence.
The judge also questioned prosecutors about Trump’s continuing public insistence that vandalism caused the damage.
“How am I to look at these statements as anything other than statements by the chief executive urging your office to pursue a prosecution that you have told me is meritless?” Edelman asked during the September hearing.
Thursday’s order resolved the remaining issue in Hearn’s favor.
Prosecutors acknowledged flawed installation
Hearn was arrested after stopping at the Reflecting Pool during a June 19 bicycle ride.
He said he noticed the pool’s newly applied coating peeling and reached into the water to examine a loose section that remained attached to the side. Hearn said he released it when a park employee told him to do so.
Prosecutors initially took a considerably different view.
A grand jury indicted Hearn on one felony count of malicious destruction of property, an offense carrying a maximum sentence of 10 years. Pirro publicly accused him of “forcefully and violently” ripping material from the pool and said prosecutors would prove his guilt beyond a reasonable doubt.
The case began unraveling after prosecutors obtained additional Interior Department records.
Those documents showed repeated problems with the installation of the Reflecting Pool’s new lining and extensive peeling throughout the basin.
A National Park Service engineer had warned in a June 11 email—eight days before Hearn’s encounter at the pool—that overspray along the perimeter could create a one- to two-foot strip “that is vulnerable to peeling.” That was the same general area where Hearn was accused of damaging the liner.
Prosecutors also found damage in areas toward the middle of the Reflecting Pool where someone attempting to peel the lining deliberately would have been unlikely to reach.
“Given all of this newly discovered information, it is difficult to attribute the widespread damage to the Reflecting Pool to vandalism, let alone to establish that fact beyond a reasonable doubt,” Pirro’s office said when it moved to drop the charge.
$16 million project suffered problems
The Reflecting Pool had undergone a major renovation ahead of America’s 250th anniversary celebrations.
Atlantic Industrial Coatings received more than $14.6 million to resurface the landmark, according to federal contracting records reviewed by ABC News. The contract was awarded through a no-bid process in part because officials wanted the project completed before the Independence Day celebrations.
Problems appeared soon after the work was completed.
Sections of the new blue coating began peeling, while algae also appeared in the water.
The Justice Department said documents eventually provided by the Interior Department pointed to “a rushed and flawed installation process,” including repeated failures of the lining while it was being installed.
Hearn’s attorneys argued prosecutors should have discovered those problems before seeking a felony indictment.
They also said a National Park Service witness had testified that the Reflecting Pool already required extensive repairs regardless of anything Hearn allegedly did. The pool was leaking more than 1 million gallons of water per week, its expansion joints had exceeded their service life, and the liner already had a tear, according to a defense filing.
Trump continued blaming vandals
The Justice Department’s reversal produced a public dispute inside the Trump administration.
Trump had repeatedly said vandals were responsible for the problems at the Reflecting Pool and accused someone of using a knife or box cutter to make a long cut in the liner.
After Pirro’s office moved to dismiss Hearn’s case, Trump criticized the prosecutor he had appointed.
“I disagree 100% with Jeanine Pirro, the U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia, on the Reflecting Pool,” Trump wrote.
“I don’t know what she was thinking? To me, it was a pure case of VANDALISM,” he added.
Trump later said Pirro had “choked” and “folded like an umbrella.”
Interior Secretary Doug Burgum also defended his department, saying it had provided prosecutors with evidence and witness testimony concerning alleged vandalism.
Those public statements became part of Hearn’s argument for permanently closing the case.
His lawyers said leaving prosecutors free to seek another indictment created an unjustified threat that political pressure could cause a prosecution the government had already acknowledged it could not prove to be resurrected.
Federal prosecutors maintained that they acted in good faith based on information available when Hearn was charged and changed course when additional evidence emerged.
Hearn’s attorneys call ruling a victory
Hearn competed in three Summer Olympics as a canoeist, recording a ninth place finish at the 1996 Atlanta Games. He lives in Bethesda, Maryland.
His attorneys welcomed Thursday’s decision.
They called the ruling “a victory for the rule of law and for an innocent American seeking justice” and said it would allow Hearn to move forward with his life.
“This administration chose to pursue an unjust prosecution against Mr. Hearn,” his attorneys said. “It should not get repeated chances to wield the power of criminal prosecution against someone who should never have been prosecuted.”
The permanent dismissal removes the possibility that the Justice Department could revive the felony property destruction charge if political or investigative circumstances changed.

Judge permanently dismisses case charging three-time Olympian with vandalizing Reflecting Pool
A judge in the nation's capital agreed on Thursday to permanently dismiss a criminal case charging a three-time Olympian with vandalizing the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, a move that could prevent federal prosecutors from reviving the case under political pressure from President Donald Trump.
Related video above: What really caused the damage to the Reflecting Pool?
D.C. Superior Court Judge Todd Edelman ordered the dismissal of David Hearn's case with "prejudice," which would block U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro's office from refiling the felony charge against him. The judge ruled nearly a month after hearing attorneys' arguments.
Hearn's lawyers say Trump administration officials have continued to falsely accuse the Maryland resident of vandalizing the reflecting pool despite Pirro's decision to drop the case on July 31. Trump responded by saying Pirro "choked" and "folded like an umbrella."
In a court filing in July, Pirro said new evidence produced by the Interior Department showed Hearn wasn't responsible for damage to the pool's lining. Pirro's office attributed the damage instead to a botched installation by a contractor as well as a rush to complete the project in time for this summer's America 250 celebration in Washington.
Pirro's admission was an embarrassing setback for the White House. Interior Secretary Doug Burgum has backed Trump's claims that vandals damaged the pool.
Hearn has said he was on a bike ride on June 19 when he reached in to examine the pool's newly peeled coating and briefly touched a chunk attached to the side of the pool. But he said he obeyed a park worker's command to let go of it.
Hearn was charged with one count of property destruction, which carries a maximum prison sentence of 10 years. His lawyers questioned whether prosecutors properly presented the grand jury with adequate evidence to support the charge and the amount of damage alleged by the government.
Hearn, 67, of Bethesda, Maryland, competed in three Summer Olympics, earning his best finish, ninth, at the 1996 Atlanta Olympic Games, the U.S. Olympic and Paralympic Committee says on its website.

DC judge says Trump’s demands to re-charge David Hearn are ‘simply fanciful’ after Jeanine Pirro already tossed ‘meritless’ case

A judge in Washington, D.C., has thrown out a criminal case against a former Olympian accused of damaging the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool — and blocked prosecutors from trying to charge him again.
U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro had already agreed to drop felony charges against 67-year-old David Hearn after she admitted that the damage was likely caused by “botched” construction. But she wanted to leave open the possibility of prosecuting Hearn again after Donald Trump’s demands.
On Thursday, the judge called that idea “simply fanciful” and permanently tossed the case.
Hearn “faces the unique possibility that the government will revive this case, one that it has already announced to be meritless — based on political pressure brought by the President of the United States upon his subordinate officers,” DC Superior Court Judge Todd Edelman wrote Thursday.
“The Court respects the authority of the Office of the United States Attorney to decide which cases to prosecute and which to dismiss,” Edelman wrote. “However, in the exceptional circumstances posed by this case, the government has no right to retain the ability to compound the errors it has already made, or even to threaten to do so, at Mr. Hearn’s expense.”
The dismissal of the case with prejudice ensures that the Department of Justice “cannot bring this case against him again,” Hearn’s lawyers said in a statement shared with The Independent.
“This decision is a victory for the rule of law and for an innocent American seeking justice,” attorneys Norm Eisen with the Democracy Defenders Fund, Mary Dohrmann of Washington Litigation Group and Steve Levin and Michael Bromwich of Steptoe LLP said in a joint statement.
“This case never should have been brought in the first place,” they added. “This was a miscarriage of justice, and what happened to Mr. Hearn is an outrage that should shock every American.”
The decision marks the likely end of a months-long legal battle after prosecutors accused Hearn of tearing out the recently applied “American flag blue” liner that started to flap to the surface shortly after it was installed earlier this year.
Weeks after she publicly accused Hearn of “forcefully and violently” ripping out the liner, Pirro’s office admitted that the sealant started to peel “almost immediately” after the work was completed.
Contractors left behind “widespread damage,” prosecutors wrote in court filings.
It was not until after the indictment was filed that the Department of Interior determined that the “damage was the result of a botched installation and not vandalism,” they wrote.
Trump, however, has demanded that Pirro re-open the case while accusing her of having “folded like an umbrella” and “choking.”
On Truth Social, Trump called Hearn’s attorney Norm Eisen a “Political Hack” and “TRUMP DERANGED SLEAZEBAG” as he pushed Pirro to “re-visit her hastily made decision” to drop the case.
Hearn — a champion canoeist who represented the U.S. at the 1992, 1996, and 2000 Summer Olympics — argued that Trump’s comments suggest the administration is trying to charge him again as part of a politically motivated attack.
Edelman hauled lawyers to court last month to hear why prosecutors would want to keep the door open to re-charging Hearn despite admitting there isn’t any evidence to do so.
The Trump administration, meanwhile, continues to funnel millions of taxpayer dollars into renovating the Reflecting Pool, bringing total costs for the project to nearly $20 million.
In July, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum said the Trump administration would not seek any new contracts after costs exploded to more than $17 million.
But federal spending records show that the National Park Service awarded a nearly $2.7 million contract last month to American Ag Energy Inc., for the maintenance, repair and rebuilding of water purification and sewage treatment equipment.
The president initially said a refurbishing project for the iconic 2,030-foot pool could be done quickly for $1.5 million in time for White House-backed Fourth of July celebrations in the nation’s capital.
But those costs quickly surged to nearly $7 million after an initial no-bid contract was handed to a Virginia-based firm. That company, Atlantic Industrial Coatings LLC, was awarded another $6.2 million in May. On June 3, the company received another $1 million, followed by more than $461,000 on June 15.
The shallow pool, which the president repeatedly promotes as “bigger than skyscrapers,” was refurbished with a shade of dark blue and outfitted with “advanced nanobubbler technology” to tackle algae blooms that have long plagued the landmark.
But shortly after workers refilled the pool, the algae returned, and the recently applied sealant in the Trump-requested blue hue started to peel and float to the surface.

sources.news_title: Judge Puts Nail in Coffin of Trump's Lincoln Reflecting Pool Case Against David Hearn
sources.text:
A judge fully dismissed the criminal case against David Hearn on Thursday that alleged the former Olympian damaged the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool in Washington, D.C.
The ruling comes roughly two months after federal prosecutors dropped the criminal case after concluding that damage to the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool was caused by flawed installation rather than vandalism. Judge Todd Edelman referenced that decision in his order dismissing the case.
"Within a month, the government recognized that its prosecution lacked merit," the dismissal said. "It reached this conclusion not because it had misidentified Mr. Hearn as the perpetrator of the alleged act, but because no crime had occurred."
Edelman added that "because the government's legitimate interest in maintaining the possibility of a future prosecution seems so marginal, and because of the extraordinary possibility that Mr. Hearn will nonetheless face a meritless, politically motivated prosecution," the court dismissed the case with prejudice. That means the case has permanently been dismissed and cannot be refiled with the same claims.
"This case never should have been brought in the first place," Hearn's attorneys said in a statement. "This was a miscarriage of justice, and what happened to Mr. Hearn is an outrage that should shock every American. This administration chose to pursue an unjust prosecution against Mr. Hearn. It should not get repeated chances to wield the power of criminal prosecution against someone who should never have been prosecuted. Today’s decision protects Mr. Hearn from that threat, allowing him to move forward with his life as he deserves.”
Newsweek reached out to Hearn for comment on Thursday. When reached for comment, the White House referred Newsweek to a series of Truth Social posts from President Donald Trump in August in which he blamed vandals for the damage to the reflecting pool.
"Look what VANDALS did to the grass connecting the vandalized World War II Monument and the vandalized Reflecting Pool, which will be opened again, and better than ever, shortly," Trump wrote. "Anybody who thinks the Reflecting Pool wasn’t vandalized should go back to Law School! The grass is being replaced shortly, and the Reflecting Pool is almost completely fixed, including the various inflow and outflow pipes, which we were saving for the end of the year, but will do now."
Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool Renovation Project
Renovations at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool have been ongoing. Trump has said his goal is to restore the pool to a cleaner and more visually appealing condition. The effort included applying a new coating to the bottom of the Reflecting Pool called "American flag blue" and combating the persistent algae blooms that have long affected the site.
However, the project quickly hit setbacks: within days of completion, algae returned to the Reflecting Pool, turning the water green and murky despite efforts to eliminate the growth.
In addition to the algae problem, Trump claimed that vandals had caused a roughly 300-foot gash in the Reflecting Pool's newly applied liner, which became a focal point of the controversy surrounding the renovation.
Hearn was detained in June by National Guard members and Park Police after reaching into the water to touch a piece of the pool's peeling liner. Federal authorities indicted him after alleging he pulled up sections of the liner.
The government initially claimed the damage exceeded $1,000, resulting in a felony charge that carried a potential prison term of up to 10 years.
Hearn, who told previously Newsweek he had been "targeted" during his arrest, has denied the allegations from the beginning.
What Happens Next
Since the case was dismissed with prejudice, it means it cannot be brought against Hearn again.
“Today’s dismissal with prejudice ensures that the DOJ cannot bring this case against him again," Hearn's attorneys said in the statement. "This decision is a victory for the rule of law and for an innocent American seeking justice."

sources.text:
The DC US attorney’s office is barred from reviving its case against a former Olympic canoeist over alleged damage to the Reflecting Pool, a judge ruled.
David Hearn “faces the unique possibility that the government will revive this case — one that it has already announced to be meritless — based on political pressure brought by the President of the United States upon his subordinate officers,” Judge Todd Edelman of the DC Superior Court wrote in the order Thursday dismissing the case with prejudice.
The ruling means Hearn will avoid future attempts by federal prosecutors to bring new charges related to damage to the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool. Hearn pleaded not guilty to one felony count of destruction of property in excess of $1,000.
“This decision is a victory for the rule of law and for an innocent American seeking justice,” Hearn’s attorneys wrote in a joint emailed statement.
US Attorney Jeanine Pirro’s office took the unusual step in July to drop the case against Hearn, but sought dismissal without prejudice. Such an order would have allowed the office to bring a similar indictment against Hearn in the future.
Edelman formally dismissed the charge in August, but asked for briefing on Hearn’s attorneys bid to have the case dismissed with prejudice.
Pirro’s office moved to drop the case based on evidence that suggested the damage to the Reflecting Pool was the result of a contractor’s flawed installation of lining to permanently seal the pool ahead of celebrations for the 250th anniversary of American independence.
President Donald Trump condemned Pirro over the move, saying his US attorney pick “folded like an umbrella.” He continues to claim the damage was the result of vandalism.
In his order, Edelman wrote that while “the government wishes to hold open the possibility of the development of evidence that would support a future prosecution, its own representations make plain that such a possibility is theoretical at best, and more likely, is simply fanciful.”
“The government has no right to retain the ability to compound the errors it has already made, or even to threaten to do so, at Mr. Hearn’s expense,” Edelman said.
Edelman on Thursday also granted Hearn’s Sept. 28 motion to admit into the court record an Aug. 31 Truth Social post from Trump arguing, “Anybody who thinks the Reflecting Pool wasn’t vandalized should go back to Law School!”
The DC US attorney’s office didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.
‘Nothing’ Can Save Case
Edelman questioned federal prosecutor Michael Spence during a Sept. 4 hearing on future plans for the case, given the office’s possession of “all the evidence that there ever would be as to the economic loss.”
Spence said the office had no plans to revive the prosecution, but if additional evidence were to come forth, “there’s no reason this court should tie the hands of a future grand jury.”
Edelman commented on the statements Trump made publicly on the case, questioning whether it puts undue pressure on the US attorney’s office to prosecute Hearn.
“How am I to look at these statements as anything other than statements by the chief executive urging your office to pursue a prosecution that you have told me is meritless and that you have no current plan in the works to make it less meritless?” Edelman said.
One of Hearn’s lawyers, Steven Levin of Steptoe LLP, said during the hearing that the US attorney’s office has failed to identify any witness or evidence that it expects to emerge to warrant future charges.
“There is nothing that can save the case that was dismissed,” Levin said.
Hearn’s lawyers noted in a July 28 supplement supporting their motion for grand jury minutes and instructions “troubling” findings in the transcripts, including shifting expert testimony about whether the damage Hearn allegedly caused was in excess of $1,000.
Former prosecutors and ethics lawyers have said Pirro’s move to dismiss the case effectively allowed the office to skirt judicial scrutiny.
Pirro, a former New York county judge and district attorney, has struggled to secure grand jury indictments and court wins as the US attorney in DC. This includes the failed prosecution against the man who went viral on social media for throwing a sandwich at a Customs and Border Protection officer during the administration’s law enforcement surge in DC.
Hearn was also represented in the case by attorneys at Democracy Defenders Fund and Washington Litigation Group.
The case is US v. Hearn, D.C. Super. Ct., No. 2026 CF2 010237, 10/1/26.

Hearn, Edelman wrote, “faces the unique possibility that the government will revive this case — one that it has already announced to be meritless — based on political pressure brought by the President of the United States upon his subordinate officers.” The government “has no right to retain the ability to compound the errors it has already made, or even to threaten to do so, at Mr. Hearn’s expense,” Edelman wrote.
Trump had lashed out at Hearn over political donations and because one of his lawyers, Norm Eisen, has been a longtime Trump critic involved in many legal battles against the administration.
Eisen and Hearn’s other attorneys — Mary Dohrmann, Steve Levin and Michael Bromwich — said in a joint statement that the decision “is a victory for the rule of law and for an innocent American seeking justice” and said the case never should have been brought in the first place.
“This was a miscarriage of justice, and what happened to Mr. Hearn is an outrage that should shock every American,” they wrote. “This administration chose to pursue an unjust prosecution against Mr. Hearn. Today’s decision protects Mr. Hearn from that threat, allowing him to move forward with his life as he deserves.”
Pirro’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Attorneys for Hearn and the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Columbia sparred in court last month over whether Hearn’s Reflecting Pool case should be dismissed with prejudice, meaning prosecutors would be barred from bringing another case against him. At the center of much of the discussion: Donald Trump’s pressure campaign on Pirro’s office and his decision to link his desire for prosecution to the political beliefs of Hearn and one of his attorneys, Norm Eisen.
Pirro’s office dropped the case in late July after evidence showed the area was already damaged, and Hearn’s team moved to ban the office from bringing another case in August.
At an unrelated press conference last month, Pirro declined to answer several questions from reporters about her handling of the Reflecting Pool case.
Pirro’s office wanted to maintain its ability to bring a theoretical case, even though its own evidence — that the section of the Reflecting Pool that Hearn allegedly touched was already damaged, and they can’t prove more than $1,000 in damage — would make bringing another felony case impossible.
“What future prosecution could even occur?” Edelman asked at the hearing.
“That I don’t know,” said Michael Spence, a career official in the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Columbia.
“Give me an example of one possible thing that could happen” to change the fundamentally flawed case, the judge asked. “Even theoretically, what could there be?”
Spence conceded he had no satisfactory answer. He added that the U.S. Attorney’s Office had no investigation going into Hearn “as of this second” but said that could change.
Edelman noted that it was going to be pretty difficult to find a case with similar circumstances to Hearn’s case, and asked Spence how he was supposed to look at Trump’s statements calling for a prosecution that Pirro’s office admits was meritless. The president’s statements, Spence said, “speak for themselves.”
Steve Levin, an attorney for Hearn, said prosecutors “had no case” and that the government abused its prosecutorial discretion by rushing to indict Hearn to please the president, misleading a grand jury along the way.
“That’s where the bad faith comes into play,” Levin said. How is Hearn supposed to trust the grand jury process, Levin asked, given that the case got through before? “There’s no confidence that Mr. Hearn has that the grand jury will do the right thing” if another case was presented,” he said.
Pirro’s office, Levin argued, is trying to keep a “discredited felony accusation on life support,” and doing so served no public interest.
“There is nothing that can save the case they dismissed,” Levin said. “The government has basically acknowledged there is nothing that can revive this case.”
But Spence said the grand jury process would still give Hearn protection from a bad faith prosecution.
“The government did act in good faith in this case,” Spence argued.

Primary Content
A judge has dismissed with prejudice the government's vandalism charges against former Olympic canoeist David Hearn. That means federal prosecutors cannot refile them in the future, despite President Trump's public demands to do so.
In fact, as D.C. Superior Court Judge Todd Edelman explained in a 26-page ruling released Thursday, the case should be permanently closed in large part because of the "political pressure brought by the President of the United States upon his subordinate officers."
"While the prosecutors admit that the evidence indicates that he committed no crime, the President's statements create a risk that Mr. Hearn will be prosecuted nonetheless, either because the current United States Attorney and her assistants will eventually yield to his public pressure campaign or because the President will replace them with prosecutors more likely to carry out his wishes," wrote Edelman, an Obama appointee.
Hearn, 67, was arrested at the Reflecting Pool in June, around the time its multimillion-dollar new blue lining started noticeably peeling off in chunks. He was charged with one felony count of property destruction and quickly indicted by a grand jury, though he pleaded not guilty.
In late July, however, with a trial start date — and the prospect of up to 10 years in prison if convicted — looming, Pirro's office abruptly asked the judge to drop the charges against Hearn and three others altogether.
Citing new reports from the Department of the Interior and National Park Service, federal prosecutors admitted that the Reflecting Pool damage was, in fact, "the result of botched installation and not vandalism."
Trump disagreed, and publicly urged Pirro to revisit the case — which Thursday's ruling prevents.
When asked for comment, the White House referred NPR to three of Trump's Truth Social posts from August, blaming the Reflecting Pool damage on vandals and disagreeing with U.S. Attorney for D.C. Jeanine Pirro's decision to drop charges against Hearn in the first place.
Neither the U.S. Attorney's Office for D.C. nor the Department of Justice returned NPR's requests for comment in time for publication.
Hearn's lawyers — Norm Eisen, Mary Dohrmann, Steve Levin and Michael Bromwich — celebrated the ruling in a joint statement, calling it "a victory for the rule of law and for an innocent American seeking justice."
"This case never should have been brought in the first place," they said. "This was a miscarriage of justice, and what happened to Mr. Hearn is an outrage that should shock every American."
The soft-spoken Maryland resident quickly became a cause célèbre for the many Americans captivated by the Reflecting Pool saga, which some saw as a referendum on the Trump administration itself.
In an August interview with NPR, Hearn described his experience as "Kafkaesque" and "Orwellian," but said he was buoyed by the support he'd received from within and beyond his community.
"With the power of the law, the power of the courts, and my wonderful team, I feel very well equipped … to bring democracy back to me," he said.
Trump's public pressure campaign
Trump railed against Pirro in the days and weeks after she dropped the charges, saying she had "choked" and "folded like an umbrella" — and didn't rule out firing her. He continued to blame the damage on vandalism and wrote on social media that anyone who disagreed "should go back to Law School."
"Most concerningly," Edelman wrote, during that time, the president also leveled increasingly personal attacks against Hearn and his legal team.
"U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro should re-visit her hastily made decision, especially since it turned out that the 'gentleman' involved is a big player in ActBlue, a disgraceful fundraising SCAM, and is represented by a TRUMP DERANGED SLEAZEBAG, Political Hack Lawyer, Norm Eisen," Trump wrote in early August, in one of the social media posts the White House directed NPR to on Thursday.
It's against that backdrop that Hearn's legal team has been lobbying the judge to dismiss the charges with prejudice, to prevent the same case from being revived. The Trump administration, on the other hand, sought to leave that door open.
Edelman's Thursday ruling offers a peek into the government's argument — and then dismantles it.
Edelman wrote that when asked in court what kind of hypothetical new evidence might prompt prosecutors to revisit the case, an unnamed assistant U.S. attorney "waxed philosophical, musing, 'I don't know what the future may bring. None of us do.'"
He says prosecutors could not provide any specific examples of such evidence, and "admitted that the government was no longer even investigating the case."
"Given its own description of the existing evidence and the circumstances of this case, the development of contrary evidence seems practically inconceivable, and the possibility of a future meritorious prosecution strikes the Court as fanciful," Edelman concluded.

The Reflecting Pool, which was drained after July 4th, remains empty and fenced off for repairs, with no public timeline for completion.

It should not get repeated chances to wield the power of criminal prosecution against someone who should never have been prosecuted. Today’s decision protects Mr. Hearn from that threat, allowing him to move forward with his life as he deserves.”
After the Trump administration spent more than $14 million to change the color of the Reflecting Pool, the new liner began peeling off. Trump blamed vandals, and four people were arrested, including Hearn, a three-time Olympic athlete who was the only person charged with a felony.

“There'll be a time and a place to discuss what the experience has been like for him. It has been difficult, as you can imagine, but he's keeping his attitude of fighting back strong,” he said.
“As you can imagine, when the most powerful people in the world say you could be going to prison for up to 10 years, make false claims about you, that's profoundly unsettling,” Eisen said. “But Davey Hearn is a three-time Olympian, multiple times world champion and canoeist. He cares about this case obviously for himself, but it's of the utmost importance to our democracy to fight back when innocent people are targeted by the regime.
